Wessex
WESS-ex
n. (the kingdom of the West Saxons, which outlasted every rival and became the kingdom of England)
Latinised from Old English West Seaxe, the West Saxons; the modern form was revived by antiquaries.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wessex was the kingdom of the West Saxons, founded, the Chronicle says, by Cerdic in 495, and the one English kingdom that survived everything. Birinus preached to its king Cynegils about 635 and set his see at Dorchester on Thames, later moved to Winchester; Aldhelm and then Boniface came out of its monasteries; Ine issued the earliest surviving West Saxon laws about 694, with clauses on baptism, Sunday work and church dues. Egbert made it the chief English kingdom in 825, and when the Danes had destroyed Northumbria, Mercia and East Anglia, Alfred held Wessex alone, bought time at Athelney, won at Edington in 878, and then set about translating books into English because he thought the collapse had come from ignorance. His house went on to rule all England. The dictionary records Wessex because its survival was not a matter of resources, which it did not have in 878, nor of probability. Scripture ascribes the frustration of great plans and the standing of God's own purpose to the same hand: the counsel of the heathen comes to nothing, the counsel of the LORD stands for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines counsel as deliberation and advice; a device as a contrived plan; to purpose as to intend; to direct as to point out a course; and a thought as an intention or design.

expand to see more

COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion given for directing the judgment or conduct of another; deliberation; consultation.

DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; a scheme formed in the mind; a stratagem.

PURPOSE, v.t. To intend; to design; to resolve; to determine on some end or object to be accomplished.

DIRECT, v.t. To point out a course to; to guide; to show the right road or course; to regulate.

THOUGHT, n. The operation of the mind; idea; conception; design; purpose; opinion.

Key Scripture

Psa 33:10 — "The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect."

Psa 33:11 — "The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations."

Isa 14:24 — "The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand:"

Pro 16:9 — "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."

Modern Corruption

The kingdom of the West Saxons, converted under Cynegils, which alone survived the Danish conquests and under Alfred's house became England.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the asymmetry between human plans and God's. The Psalmist puts the two in parallel so that the contrast is unmistakable: “The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” (Psa 33:10), while “The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations” (Psa 33:11). Wessex in the winter of 878 had nothing else to appeal to.

The live temptation, especially in an English-speaking country with a long Christian history, is to convert this into national flattery, as though Alfred's survival were a promise made to a people. The oath in Isaiah is given about God's purpose and not about anyone's nation: “Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand” (Isa 14:24). What is left to men is the planning and the walking, with the outcome withheld: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Alfred devised a great deal, and he also had the marshes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Hebrew machashabah (H4284), a thought or device; Hebrew amad (H5975), to stand; Hebrew kun (H3559), to establish.

expand to see more

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, plan; “the counsel of the heathen to nought”, Psalm 33:10.

Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a thought, a device; “the devices of the people of none effect”, Psalm 33:10.

Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, to endure; “The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever”, Psalm 33:11.

Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to purpose, to counsel; “as I have purposed, so shall it stand”, Isaiah 14:24.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to make firm; “but the LORD directeth his steps”, Proverbs 16:9.

Usage

"“The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever” (Psa 33:11) — Wessex's only asset in 878."

"“as I have purposed, so shall it stand” (Isa 14:24) — a promise about God, not a people."

"“but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9) — Alfred planned; the marshes were given."
